Plock Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Płock, Poland

Not demolished. Jews are first recorded in Płock in 1237, with a dedicated Jewish district by then. This cemetery, established around 1570 outside the city walls on land purchased by the kehilla with King Zygmunt August's consent (November 26, 1568), faced significant local resistance, prompting royal interventions from both Zygmunt August (1570) and Stefan Batory (1576) to protect its establishment. It remained active until 1850. By 1921, 7,352 Jews lived in Płock; in 1941, most were deported via Działdowo to ghettos in Drzewica, Kielce, Przysucha, and Tomaszów Mazowiecki, before murder at Treblinka in 1942. A 1946 postwar Jewish Committee registered 333 people. Germans devastated this cemetery during WWII, using tombstones for road hardening and stairs, including at an Evangelical church and the seminary that housed the SS; Communist-era development built a high school boarding house and park on the grounds. A 2018 student mural now commemorates the site.
